entities.summary: Freydís Eiríksdóttir was an Icelandic woman said to be the daughter of Erik the Red, who figured prominently in the Norse exploration of North America as an early colonist of Vinland, while her brother, Leif Erikson, is credited in early histories of the region with the first European contact. The medieval and primary sources that mention Freydís are the two Vinland sagas: the Saga of the Greenlanders and the Saga of Erik the Red. The two sagas offer differing accounts, though Freydís is portrayed in both as one of the strongest female Vikings.

entities.name: Freydís Eiríksdóttir
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Freydís Eiríksdóttir was an Icelandic-Norse woman, said to be the daughter of Erik the Red, who figured prominently in two Norse sagas describing the early exploration and colonization of Vinland (North America). She is one of the most vivid female figures in the Icelandic saga literature — both as a warrior who defended herself against Skraelings (indigenous people) and as a villain who reportedly orchestrated the murder of her fellow colonists.

Freydís appears in both the Grænlendinga saga and Eiríks saga rauða, though with different characterizations. In the Grænlendinga saga, she is a heroic figure: when the Norse Vinland colonists fled from attacking Skraelings, a pregnant Freydís alone stood her ground, baring her breast and striking her sword against it — so terrifying the attackers that they retreated. In the same saga, however, she is also portrayed as the instigator of a massacre of her fellow colonists, including the women, whom she killed herself when the men refused.

The historicity of both episodes is uncertain, but Freydís is likely based on a real woman who participated in the Vinland expeditions (c. 1000–1010 CE). Her story represents the intersection of two important historical threads: the Norse reaching North America five centuries before Columbus, and the rare visibility of women in saga-age Norse exploration. She is one of very few named women in the historical record of Viking exploration and has become a significant figure in modern feminist retellings of Norse history.
